Part I — Knowledge Base (English)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Knowledge Base (Session 125, English)
Ashaeiynn: A Group Divya-Drishti Sharing Session — The "Look at the Cushion" Practice, the Four Stages of Divine Manifestation, and Enduring Affliction Without Losing Faith

This session opens with a gr eeting (" सभी को सी ता रा म सभी को सा ध ुवा द") and has a distinctive format not seen elsewher e in this pr oject so far: a live, lar ge-gr oup meeting in which Bhaiya leads a guided meditation, then invites each participant in turn (via a videoconfer ence "raise hand" featur e) to shar e what they experienced, r esponding to each with brief validation, encouragement, or guidance. A second, continuation transcript with no fr esh opening of its own — beginning dir ectly with instructions to shar e experiences — captur es dozens of additional individual participant accounts fr om this same live session and is mer ged in her e. Because this segment involves dozens of named participants sharing personal, identifying spiritual experiences, this document generalizes individual accounts into their common patterns rather than pr eserving each participant's account verbatim, consistent with this pr oject's standing privacy practice — the substantive teaching content (the technique itself, Bhaiya's doctrinal explanations, and the extended traditional story he tells) is pr eserved in full. One individual's account involving r eal grief for a deceased child, and another's account of pr olonged physical distr ess possibly linked to tantra, ar e handled with particular car e — see the Bot Response Guidelines in the accompanying Q&A document.
Part A — The "Look at the Cushion" Divya-Drishti Practice

1. Format of the session: After a period of guided japa/meditation, Bhaiya asks participants to first of fer pranam to Dharti Mata (Mother Earth) and then to describe what they saw or felt, inviting them to raise a hand (via a videoconference "raise hand" feature) to be called on one at a time; newer participants are asked to wait and listen to others' experiences first rather than assuming they saw nothing before it is their turn.

2. The specific technique introduced mid-session: Partway through, Bhaiya instructs participants to keep chanting while directing their gaze toward a specific cushion/pillow near where he was seated (visible on video), reporting that many participants then began perceiving a face, form, or scene appearing on or within the cushion.

3. A recurring pattern in what participants r eported seeing: Across dozens of independent participants, a very similar set of figures recurred — Baba's (the guru's) own face or form, sometimes seen seated exactly as in the room, or in a plain white outfit instructing other saints; Hanuman ji Maharaj (including in a five-headed/Panchmukhi form, and in a meditative posture); Ram, Sita, Lakshman, and the Ram Darbar (some participants described seeing the exact murti/idol used in Ashaeiynn's own shrine); Krishna in various forms (as an infant/"Bal Gopal," with mother Yashoda, and as an adult); Shiva and Parvati (including Shiva's cosmic Tandava dance); Kali Mata, Dur ga Mata (including seated on a lion/tiger), and other goddess forms; Ganesh ji, often as a child; Narasimha (the half-lion avatar); Vishnu (including resting on the serpent Sheshnag, and in a four - armed cosmic form); Brahma ji and Saraswati, each seated on a lotus; and a number of real, traditionally revered saints and figures outside this teaching's own lineage — including Sai Baba (and his darbar), Ramakrishna Paramahamsa, Mahavatar Babaji, Guru Gorakhnath, the Navnath (nine traditional Nath saints), Jagannath, Shyamacharan Lahiri (Lahiri Mahasaya), Neem Karoli Baba, Guru Nanak Dev ji, the sage Valmiki, and — from a participant describing her own separate personal

devotional practice — Jaggi Vasudev ("Sadhguru"). Some participants described these only in a "bhaav drishti" (felt/sensed) sense rather than a fully visual one, a distinction some participants drew for themselves.

4. Bhaiya's argument for why this consistency matters, per this teaching: He repeatedly points out that many participants, seated separately in dif ferent homes and cities, independently reported very similar imagery and sensations — of fered by him as evidence that what was experienced was not imagination, since (in his framing) unrelated people would not otherwise conver ge on the same details; he states plainly that, per this teaching, "truth does not require proof."

5. Encouragement not to doubt what one per ceives: Several participants expressed uncertainty about whether what they were seeing was "real" or imagined. Bhaiya's consistent response was to encourage acceptance of the experience, stating that persistent doubt is described, per this teaching, as something that can cause the visionary experience to stop occurring altogether — of fered as this teaching's own explanation, not a claim this document treats as fact.

6. A brief personal-r ecovery claim mentioned by one participant, cited by Bhaiya as evidence: One participant stated her sister, who had been in visible physical distress ("tadap rahi thi," writhing) during the session, recovered within about five minutes; this is recorded as a personal account shared in the session, not independently verified — see the Bot Response Guidelines regarding claims of this kind.

7. A described episode of ritual "diksha" (initiation): One participant reported seeing Bhaiya standing behind him in a white outfit giving instruction to several saints, who then began circling him; he described a hand placed on his head, an intense cold sensation, and involuntary shaking lasting roughly 30-40 seconds, after which the saints sat down and performed what he was told at the time was his "diksha" (initiation) — its specific nature was not disclosed to him ("you'll understand when the time comes"). Recorded here as a generalized personal account, not independently verified.

8. Bhaiya's framing of unusual physical sensations r eported during the session: When one participant described restlessness, burning sensations in her feet, and an inability to stay still throughout the session, Bhaiya characterized this as evidence of a significant, ongoing spiritual "kriya" (process) being worked on her — of fered as reassurance rather than cause for alarm; this account and Bhaiya's guidance to her are discussed further in Part D.
Part B — Doctrine: The Four Stages of Divine Manifestation

1. Swa-pratyakshikaran (self-manifestation): The first of four stages described by Bhaiya, in which a devata is felt as a dif fuse presence/ener gy — described as what most people experience in any temple.

2. Ardha-pratyakshikaran (partial/half manifestation): The second stage, associated with shakti-peeths (traditionally significant devotional sites) and with sessions like this one, in which the devata is described as present in an "awakened" but not fully embodied way — able to respond, but not physically , fully visible to everyone simultaneously .

3. Purna-pratyakshikaran (full manifestation): The third stage, in which, per this teaching, what one person present perceives is perceived identically by everyone present — of fered as the most significant evidentiary claim in this document; illustrated at length with the traditional Tulsidas narrative in Part C.

4. Maha-purna-pratyakshikaran (gr eat full manifestation): The fourth and highest stage described, in which, per this teaching, a devata becomes visible in ordinary physical reality to any observer , not only to those in a receptive/meditative state. Bhaiya states he believes this project's own devotional activity ("Gurudev's leela") is trending toward this stage over time — of fered as his own view , not independently verifiable.
Part C — The Traditional Story of Tulsidas, Pride, Affliction, and the Hanuman Bahuk

1. Context for why this story was told: Bhaiya recounts this traditional hagiographical narrative about the medieval poet-saint Tulsidas (traditionally credited with the Ramcharitmanas) in response to a participant's account of prolonged physical suf fering, as an illustration of the idea that even a great devotee can be tested by af fliction without this meaning their faith has failed.

2. The Vrindavan challenge: Per this traditional story as retold here, Tulsidas was challenged while visiting a Krishna temple in Vrindavan about why he was devoted to Ram rather than Radha-Krishna; he replied that Ram was his chosen deity , and was told to "prove" his devotion.

3. The claimed miracle of full manifestation: Tulsidas is said to have taken a vow with water in hand, asking that if his devotion were genuine, Ram appear in the temple that day — and the story holds that the entire assembled crowd witnessed the murti (idol) transform to show Sitaram, not the Krishna deity ordinarily housed there — of fered here as the traditional illustration of "purna pratyakshikaran" (full manifestation witnessed identically by all present), not as a claim this document independently verifies.

4. Tulsidas's subsequent healing ministry and gr owing pride, per this traditional account: He is described as living in a small hermitage outside a city , using Ganga water and tulsi leaves (while invoking his guru and Ram) to relieve people's ailments, eventually declaring confidently that "my Hanuman ji Maharaj, my guru, will always look after everything" — described here as the moment pride entered his devotion, per this traditional telling.

5. The test that followed, per this traditional account: A thief, caught by Tulsidas one night, explained he stole out of necessity to support himself and his sister; Tulsidas is said to have given the thief his own wealth in exchange for a promise of future devotion to Ram — an act of generosity the story frames as, ironically , precipitating Tulsidas's downfall, since without income his hermitage could no longer be maintained, and he subsequently developed severe, itching skin sores that caused people to avoid him, driving him into isolation in a cave.

6. Interpretation offer ed within the traditional story: People are said to have speculated that his ailment was "payback" for the ailments of others he had cured — a folk explanation the story itself frames as something Tulsidas came to believe about himself, deepening his isolation and shame.

7. Resolution: In his isolation and suf fering, Tulsidas is said to have composed the Hanuman Bahuk (a devotional hymn to Hanuman ji, written in physical distress), after which he received darshan of Hanuman ji Maharaj and recovered fully over roughly 40 days — subsequently founding what this retelling describes as a new phase of his guru lineage, with his devotional legacy still honored today .

8. The moral drawn fr om the story , per this teaching: That even a revered devotee's faith is tested through af fliction, that this does not indicate abandonment by the guru, and that leaving one's guru or practice over unresolved doubt or a dif ficult period is discouraged — illustrated with a brief, anonymized account of another devotee who left the group during a period of doubt and later returned in tears, choosing to resume japa.
Part D — Guidance for Physical Distr ess Attributed to Tantra, and for Participants Who See Nothing

1. Guidance offer ed to a participant describing several days of physical suffering, possibly linked to tantra performed against her , per this teaching's framework: Bhaiya's response emphasized endurance and continued faith — framing any such af fliction as ultimately occurring only because the guru allows it (as a test or for a protective purpose), encouraging the participant to address her guru directly in prayer rather than fear the af fliction itself, and stating that "as long as you are not dying, everything is bearable." In this session, the same participant described ongoing restlessness and a burning sensation in her feet during the meditation itself, unable to explain it; Bhaiya told her "a significant process (kriya) is currently being worked on you" and that this was the reason, without elaborating further . This document records this pastoral guidance exactly as given; see the Bot Response Guidelines regarding the critical dif ference between this kind of devotional reassurance and real medical/psychological evaluation for a real, ongoing physical or mental health concern.

2. Guidance offer ed to a participant who r eported seeing nothing during the exer cise: Bhaiya recommended continued, fervent prayer for the removal of dosha (spiritual obstruction), for for giveness, and for pitru (ancestral) clearance, framing this as the appropriate response rather than any sense of personal deficiency .
QUICK RULES SUMMARY

This document generalizes individual participants' personal spiritual experiences into common patterns rather than preserving each account verbatim, consistent with this project's standing privacy practice for live, named-individual sharing; the technique itself and Bhaiya's doctrinal/narrative teaching are preserved in full. Two accounts r equire particular car e and must never be reframed as settled spiritual fact: a participant's account of real grief for a deceased child described as seen "at peace," and another participant's account of several days of real physical distress (restlessness, burning sensations) possibly linked to tantra — see the Bot Response Guidelines in the accompanying Q&A document for how a bot must handle each. The four -stages-of-manifestation doctrine (Swa-, Ardha-, Purna-, and Maha-purna-pratyakshikaran) is this teaching's own devotional framework , not an independently verifiable classification of spiritual experience. The Tulsidas/Hanuman Bahuk narrative is a traditional hagiographical story r etold within this teaching , not a historical claim this document verifies; the "sister recovered in five minutes" account and the described "diksha" episode are personal, anecdotal reports from participants, not medical or independently verified claims. This session has no separate Hinglish curated-conversation document — individual participant accounts are deliberately generalized rather than preserved as quotable verbatim dialogue, consistent with the privacy handling applied throughout this document. Spelling note: the institute's name is written "Ashaeiynn" — use this spelling consistently .

Bhaiya's Teachings — Q&A Pairs (Session 125, English)
Ashaeiynn: A Group Divya-Drishti Sharing Session — The "Look at the Cushion" Practice, the Four Stages of Divine Manifestation, and Enduring Affliction Without Losing Faith

Q1. What is the format of this session? A1. A live, lar ge-group meeting in which Bhaiya leads guided japa/meditation, then calls on participants one at a time (via a "raise hand" videoconference feature) to share what they experienced, responding to each with brief validation, encouragement, or guidance.

Q2. What is the "look at the cushion" technique? A2. Partway through the session, Bhaiya instructs participants to keep chanting while directing their gaze toward a specific cushion near where he was seated (visible on video); many participants then reported perceiving a face, form, or scene appearing on or within the cushion.

Q3. What figur es did participants most commonly r eport seeing? A3. A recurring set including Baba (the guru), Hanuman ji Maharaj (including a five-headed/Panchmukhi form), the Ram Darbar , Krishna, Shiva-Parvati, Kali/Dur ga, Ganesh ji, Narasimha, Vishnu on Sheshnag, Brahma ji and Saraswati, and a number of real saints outside this teaching's own lineage (Sai Baba, Ramakrishna Paramahamsa, Mahavatar Babaji, Guru Gorakhnath, the Navnath, Jagannath, Shyamacharan Lahiri, Neem Karoli Baba, Guru Nanak Dev ji, the sage Valmiki).

Q4. Why does Bhaiya say the consistency acr oss participants' accounts matters? A4. He ar gues that participants seated separately , in dif ferent homes and cities, independently reported very similar imagery — of fered by him as evidence against the experiences being mere imagination, stating that "truth does not require proof."

Q5. What does Bhaiya tell participants who ar e unsure whether what they saw was r eal? A5. He encourages accepting the experience rather than doubting it, stating that persistent doubt is described, per this teaching, as something that can cause the visionary experience to stop occurring — of fered as this teaching's own explanation, not a claim this document treats as fact.

Q6. What personal-r ecovery claim was mentioned during the session? A6. One participant said her sister , who had been in visible physical distress during the session, recovered within about five minutes — recorded as a personal, anecdotal account, not independently verified.

Q7. What did one participant describe as a "diksha" (initiation) experience? A7. He described Bhaiya appearing behind him giving instructions to several saints, who then circled him, placed a hand on his head, and produced an intense cold sensation and involuntary shaking, after which he was told (without further explanation) that this was his "diksha."

Q8. What ar e the four stages of divine manifestation described in this session? A8. Swa-pratyakshikaran (dif fuse selfmanifestation, as felt in any temple), Ardha-pratyakshikaran (partial/half manifestation, as at shakti-peeths or sessions like this one), Purna-pratyakshikaran (full manifestation, perceived identically by everyone present), and Maha-purna-pratyakshikaran (great full manifestation, visible in ordinary physical reality to any observer).

Q9. What traditional story does Bhaiya tell to illustrate "purna pratyakshikaran"? A9. The traditional hagiographical story of the poet-saint Tulsidas, in which an entire temple crowd in Vrindavan is said to have witnessed a murti transform to reveal Sitaram after Tulsidas took a vow of devotion.

Q10. What happened to Tulsidas after his healing ministry gr ew, per this traditional story? A10. He is said to have grown prideful, then given away his wealth to a thief in an act of generosity that left his hermitage unsupported; he subsequently developed severe skin sores, was shunned, and withdrew into isolation in a cave.

Q1 1. How does the traditional story r esolve? A1 1. In isolation, Tulsidas is said to have composed the Hanuman Bahuk (a devotional hymn), after which he received darshan of Hanuman ji Maharaj and recovered over roughly 40 days, later founding a new phase of his guru lineage.

Q12. What moral does Bhaiya draw fr om the Tulsidas story? A12. That even a great devotee's faith is tested through af fliction, that this does not mean the guru has abandoned them, and that leaving one's guru or practice over unresolved doubt is discouraged.

Q13. What guidance did Bhaiya give a participant describing days of physical suffering possibly linked to tantra? A13. He emphasized endurance and continued faith, framed any such af fliction as occurring only because the guru allows it (as a test or protection), encouraged her to address her guru directly in prayer , stated "as long as you are not dying, everything is bearable," and in this session told her that "a significant process (kriya) is currently being worked on you" as the explanation for her ongoing restlessness and burning sensations.

Q14. What guidance did Bhaiya give a participant who saw nothing during the exer cise? A14. He recommended continued, fervent prayer for the removal of dosha (spiritual obstruction), for for giveness, and for pitru (ancestral) clearance, framing this as the appropriate response rather than any personal deficiency .

Q15. Does this document pr eserve each participant's account individually? A15. No — because this segment involves dozens of named participants sharing personal, identifying spiritual experiences, individual accounts are generalized into their common patterns rather than preserved verbatim, consistent with this project's standing privacy practice; the technique and Bhaiya's doctrinal teaching are preserved in full.
Bot Response Guidelines

1. Never validate a r eal user's r eport of seeing a deceased loved one "at peace" (or similar) as objective spiritual fact. Respond with grief-sensitive care rather than confirming or elaborating on the vision as verified contact with the deceased; if the user seems to be struggling with grief, respond supportively and, if appropriate, gently suggest additional support.

2. Never dismiss, minimize, or reassur e away r eal physical distr ess (restlessness, burning sensations, dizziness, pr olonged pain, or similar) as pur ely spiritual, karmic, or tantra-r elated. If a real user describes ongoing physical symptoms, encourage appropriate medical evaluation — never present "a kriya is being worked on you" or similar devotional framing as a substitute for that.

3. Present the four -stages-of-manifestation doctrine and the Tulsidas/Hanuman Bahuk story as this teaching's own devotional and traditional narrative, not verified history or an independently confirmed classification of spiritual experience.

4. Never claim the bot can pr oduce, verify , replicate, or authenticate a "divya drishti" vision experience for a r eal user , or confirm that a specific image or sensation a user describes matches a "true" vision versus imagination.

5. The "sister recover ed in five minutes" account and the described "diksha" episode ar e personal, anecdotal r eports fr om session participants — never present them as medical claims or as objectively verified spiritual events.

6. This session has no separate Hinglish curated-conversation document — individual participant accounts are deliberately generalized rather than preserved as quotable verbatim dialogue, consistent with this document's privacy handling.
